practice: repeat create and save a new project with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record and stop what you will learn: complete record and stop independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: r starts recording. space stops recording or playback. connect the microphone and reduce background noise. press r once and speak a short practice sentence. press space to stop. press ctrl+s to save the project. what should happen: recording feedback and a changing time position. if that does not happen: stop before trying again. check the selected input device and whether another application controls the microphone. practice: repeat record and stop with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. play and navigate what you will learn: complete play and navigate independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: space plays or stops. p pauses or resumes. home moves to the track start. end moves to the track end. press home. press space and listen from the beginning. press p to pause at a point you want to inspect. press p again to continue or space to stop. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: confirm that an audio track exists and the audacity window is active. practice: repeat play and navigate with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos select and delete unwanted audio what you will learn: complete select and delete unwanted audio independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: shift+right arrow or shift+left arrow extends a selection in small steps. delete removes the confirmed selection. ctrl+z undoes. press ctrl+s to protect the project. move playback near the unwanted sound and stop. hold shift while using an arrow key to extend the selection. use audacityâ€™s selection toolbar or screen-reader feedback to verify start and end times. press delete, then listen across the edit. press ctrl+z immediately if the wrong audio was removed. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo and create a smaller selection. never delete an unverified range. practice: repeat select and delete unwanted audio with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record a second track what you will learn: complete record a second track independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: shift+r starts recording on a new track in current audacity versions. save the project and move to the intended start time. press shift+r. record the second part and press space to stop. use track navigation and solo or mute controls to review tracks separately. save again. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo the new recording and confirm audacityâ€™s recording preference and active track. practice: repeat record a second track with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. export an mp3 or wav file what you will learn: complete export an mp3 or wav file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: use alt+f to open file, then choose export audio. press ctrl+s to save the editable project. open file and choose export audio. choose mp3 for a smaller listening copy or wav for higher-quality uncompressed audio. select the destination and enter a new filename. review format settings and activate export. open the exported file and verify its duration and sound. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: keep the project open. check the destination, filename, format, and any error dialog. practice: repeat export an mp3 or wav file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. apply an effect safely what you will learn: complete apply an effect safely independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: select audio, open the effect menu with alt+c in many audacity versions, and choose an effect by name. save a backup project. select only the audio that should change. open the effect menu and choose the effect. preview it when available. apply it, listen again, and use ctrl+z if the result is worse. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel the dialog rather than accepting settings you do not understand. practice: repeat apply an effect safely with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. quick command list r: record shift+r: record a new track space: play or stop p: pause or resume home / end: start / end ctrl+s: save project ctrl+z: undo delete: remove selected audio return to manuals

entries.title: Accessible Job Search Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible Job Search Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: accessible job search screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual accessible job search screen reader manual keyboard-first employment skills independent self-study guide for finding and applying for work all manuals table of contents start of manual first-time keyboard guide use this short routine before following the accessible job search screen reader manual procedures. it explains exactly how the keyboard directions in this manual work. press a single key find the named key without pressing it if possible. press and release the key one time. do not hold it unless the step specifically says to hold it. stop and listen to the full screen-reader announcement before pressing another key. press a keyboard combination when a command contains a plus sign, such as ctrl+s, hold down the first key. while continuing to hold the first key, press and release the final key once. release the first key. the plus sign is not a key and should not be pressed. listen for the expected result described in the procedure. if nothing changes, verify that the correct application or webpage has focus and try the command once more. press a sequence of keys when keys are separated by commas or the word â€œthen,â€ press and release them in order instead of holding them together. after each key, listen for a menu, tab, control, or new screen before continuing. if the announcement does not match the step, press escape once to close the current menu or dialog and restart that procedure. know which navigation key to try tab and shift+tab: move forward and backward among buttons, links, fields, and other controls. arrow keys: move inside menus, lists, groups of choices, text, and many screen-reader reading views. enter: opens the selected item or activates the focused command. space: activates many buttons and checks or clears checkboxes. in a text field, space types a space. escape: cancels or closes the current menu, list, or dialog without intentionally accepting a change. verify before moving on listen for the window, page, or application name so you know where focus is. perform only one numbered step. compare what the screen reader announces with the â€œwhat should happenâ€ information in the procedure. if the result is wrong, stop. use the procedureâ€™s recovery directions, escape to cancel, or ctrl+z to undo when that command is supported. continue only after you can identify the result. save completed work with ctrl+s whenever the application supports saving. first complete independent workflow this rehearsal joins existing procedures into one uninterrupted session without repeating their directions. follow the linked procedure when a step names it, then return here for the next verification. safety check: confirm the active application, document or project name, and save location before changing content. open accessible job search screen reader manual and wait until its name, starting screen, or connected-device status is announced. choose a fictional, public, disposable, or instructor-provided practice item. do not use private client, student, medical, financial, or account-recovery information. open 1.1 create an application tracker. read its â€œwhat you will learn,â€ â€œbefore you begin,â€ keyboard-command, and expected-result information before pressing anything. complete that procedure one numbered action at a time. after each key, stop and identify what changed before continuing. state the result aloud or record it in a practice note. if it differs from â€œwhat should happen,â€ use that procedureâ€™s recovery directions before advancing. continue directly to 2.1 check resume reading order without closing the application or device session. first confirm that focus, account, file, book, conversation, or project context is still correct. complete the second procedure and verify the resulting name, state, location, permission, value, or content. do not rely only on a success sound. save or synchronize when the product supports it. wait for the completed state before disconnecting a device, closing a browser, or switching accounts. continue to 3.1 upload a resume reliably. use the exact command listed there; if the command varies by model or version, use keyboard help, the productâ€™s shortcut list, or the linked official reference instead of guessing. introduce one harmless recoverable error, such as opening the wrong menu or moving focus away. press escape once, identify the active window or device area, and return to the correct step. review the finished practice item from its beginning. confirm its title or filename, structure, content, destination, sharing state, and saved or synchronized status as applicable. close and reopen the item or return to it from the productâ€™s main screen. the workflow is complete only when you can locate it and verify the same result independently. success standard: complete all three linked tasks, explain the commands used, recover from the practice error, and locate the finished result without another person directing the next key. purpose: this manual teaches an independent, accessible workflow for finding jobs, evaluating postings, preparing resumes, completing online applications, requesting application-process accommodations when needed, and interviewing with common digital tools. platforms: the main desktop examples use windows with jaws, nvda, or narrator, but the workflow also applies to voiceover and talkback. dedicated sections cover linkedin and indeed, while company career sites are treated as variable third-party systems. legal scope: the accommodation section provides general u.s. employment-access information and practical communication guidance, not individualized legal advice. how to use this manual build your resume and reusable application information before starting a live application. open every job posting in a separate tab or save the link so you can return to it while applying. read the entire job description before investing time in the application. keep a private application tracker with employer, role, date, link, status, contact, and next action. use headings, landmarks, form controls, and browser find rather than only tab through long pages. when an application is inaccessible, document the barrier and use the employer accommodation/contact route rather than repeatedly fighting the same control. never pay an employer or recruiter to apply, receive equipment, cash a check, buy gift cards, or release a job offer. before interviews, test the meeting platform, microphone, camera if used, screen reader, headphones, and any requested accommodation. table of contents part 1 - build a job-search workspace part 2 - prepare an accessible resume part 3 - resume file formats and uploads part 4 - read a job posting efficiently part 5 - evaluate qualifications and essential functions part 6 - search on linkedin with a screen reader part 7 - apply on linkedin part 8 - search and apply on indeed part 9 - company career sites and ats systems part 10 - online application forms part 11 - dropdowns, date pickers, autocomplete, and custom controls part 12 - resume parsing and re-entering work history part 13 - cover letters and application questions part 14 - assessments and timed tests part 15 - requesting an application accommodation part 16 - disability disclosure and interview boundaries part 17 - job-search scams part 18 - email and recruiter communication part 19 - interview scheduling part 20 - zoom, teams, and video interviews part 21 - interview preparation with a screen reader part 22 - after the interview part 23 - application tracking and follow-up part 24 - mobile job search part 25 - troubleshooting inaccessible applications part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference checklists part 28 - official resources part 1 - build a job-search workspace create a folder named job search with subfolders for resume, cover letters, applications, and interview notes. keep one master resume and create role-specific copies from it. keep a plain-text file with frequently requested information: employment dates, supervisor names, addresses, phone numbers, education dates, certifications, and references. keep a private application tracker. do not store social security numbers, passwords, full banking details, or identity documents in the tracker. use a professional email address that you check regularly. 1.1 create an application tracker what you will learn: track jobs so you know what you applied to and what comes next. before you begin: open excel, google sheets, or another accessible spreadsheet. exactly how to do it create columns for employer, job title, job id, location, date found, date applied, source/link, contact, status, follow-up date, and notes. enter one practice job. save the tracker in your job search folder. after every application, update the status immediately. what should happen: you can answer â€œwhat have i applied to?â€ without searching your email. if that does not happen: if a spreadsheet is cumbersome, use a simple word table or structured text list instead. practice: track three practice postings. part 2 - prepare an accessible resume use real word headings for major sections such as summary, skills, experience, and education. use simple one-column reading order. prefer standard fonts and ordinary text over text boxes, floating shapes, icons, charts, or infographic skill bars. use actual bullet lists for achievements. write employer, job title, dates, and accomplishments as text that reads logically linearly. do not use color alone to communicate meaning. use meaningful link text for linkedin/portfolio links. run word accessibility checker before exporting. 2.1 check resume reading order what you will learn: make sure the resume reads correctly from top to bottom. before you begin: open the resume in word. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home. use ctrl+down arrow or your screen reader reading commands to move through the document. listen for each section in the intended order. use the screen reader heading list to verify section headings. use tab to identify hyperlinks and confirm their text is meaningful. run review > check accessibility and fix relevant issues. what should happen: the resume makes sense without visual position cues. if that does not happen: if information is announced out of order, remove text boxes/columns and rebuild that area in normal paragraphs or a simple table. practice: read your resume from top to bottom without using sighted layout cues. part 3 - resume file formats and uploads task how docx usually best when the employer explicitly requests word or when an ats parses word documents well. pdf useful when you want layout preserved; export from an accessible source and verify the pdf has real selectable/tagged text. plain text useful as a fallback for copy/paste fields; not usually the primary polished resume. image/scanned pdf avoid. it may be unreadable and difficult for ats/screen readers. 3.1 upload a resume reliably what you will learn: use a file-upload control without losing your place. before you begin: keep the resume in a known folder with a clear filename. exactly how to do it focus the upload resume or choose file button. press enter or space. in the file chooser, press ctrl+l if needed to type the folder path, or use the normal file explorer navigation. find the resume filename. press enter. return to the application and listen for the uploaded filename or success message. if the site parsed your resume into fields, review every parsed field before submission. what should happen: the correct filename is attached and the application recognizes it. if that does not happen: if the filename is not announced, inspect nearby status text or re-focus the upload control. do not assume the upload worked. practice: upload a disposable resume copy to a safe form or practice environment. part 4 - read a job posting efficiently 4.1 build a posting summary what you will learn: extract the facts you need before applying. before you begin: open the job posting. exactly how to do it use h or your screen reader heading-navigation command to find the job title and major sections. use browser find (ctrl+f) for terms such as salary, location, remote, qualifications, required, preferred, schedule, travel, clearance, license, benefits, and accommodation. read the entire responsibilities and qualifications sections. write down the job id/requisition number. copy the posting link into your tracker. note the closing date if one is listed. what should happen: you can summarize the job without rereading the entire page. if that does not happen: if headings are poor, use browser find and landmarks/form controls instead. practice: summarize one posting in five lines. part 5 - evaluate qualifications and essential functions separate clearly required qualifications from preferred qualifications. do not automatically reject yourself because you do not meet every preferred item. focus on whether you can perform the jobâ€™s essential functions, with or without reasonable accommodation where applicable. distinguish a true job function from one particular way an employer currently performs it. prepare examples that demonstrate transferable skills. u.s. access principle: department of labor guidance emphasizes evaluating whether a qualified applicant can perform essential functions with or without reasonable accommodation, and recognizes that there are often multiple ways to accomplish the same task. part 6 - search on linkedin with a screen reader 6.1 search linkedin jobs what you will learn: use linkedinâ€™s current accessible job-search flow. before you begin: sign in to linkedin in a supported browser. exactly how to do it activate jobs from the linkedin navigation. move backward from the jobs link or navigate to the job-search input near the top of the page. type the role, skills, location, or natural-language search you want. use up/down arrow through suggestions when linkedin announces them. tab to the search button and press enter or space. navigate by headings to the heading that represents your search. move into the result list and open a job with enter. read the job details before applying. what should happen: linkedin displays the result list and screen reader focus can move into job details. if that does not happen: linkedin changes dynamically; if focus becomes confusing, return to the jobs heading/search field and rebuild context rather than tabbing endlessly. practice: search for two roles and open one job detail page. linkedin current guidance: linkedin publishes a dedicated â€œfind jobs on linkedin - best practices for users with a screen readerâ€ article and supports screen-reader navigation of search suggestions, results, details, and application flows. part 7 - apply on linkedin 7.1 complete a linkedin application what you will learn: distinguish linkedin-hosted applications from external company applications. before you begin: open a linkedin job detail page. exactly how to do it find the apply now or apply button. activate it. if linkedin opens an in-site application dialog, review the profile-sharing option, then continue. move through each form field with tab/shift+tab and form-field navigation. upload the correct resume. answer screening questions. use the review step if offered. read name, email, phone, resume filename, and critical answers one final time. activate submit application. listen for confirmation and update your tracker. what should happen: the application is submitted and confirmation is available. if that does not happen: if apply opens the companyâ€™s external site, treat it as a new application system and use part 9. practice: complete a practice review without submitting, where possible. 7.2 set open to work carefully what you will learn: control who can see your job-search status. before you begin: be signed in to linkedin. exactly how to do it open your profile. find open to. choose finding a new job. enter desired titles, workplaces, locations, start date, and job types. find choose who sees youâ€™re open. review all linkedin members versus recruiters only. select the privacy level you intend. save/add to profile. what should happen: linkedin stores the job preferences with the visibility choice you selected. if that does not happen: do not assume â€œopen to workâ€ is private unless you explicitly review who can see it. practice: inspect the visibility control and decide which option fits your situation. part 8 - search and apply on indeed current supported combinations: indeed currently lists jaws with chrome and nvda with chrome on windows, voiceover with safari on mac/ios, and talkback with chrome on android among its supported assistive-technology combinations. 8.1 search indeed what you will learn: find jobs and preserve a predictable browser workflow. before you begin: open indeed and sign in if you use an account. exactly how to do it navigate to the job-title/keyword search field. enter a role, skill, or employer. move to the location field and enter a location or remote preference. activate search. use headings and links to review results. open a promising result in a new tab when practical so the result list remains available. read the entire description and application instructions. what should happen: you can compare multiple jobs without losing the search page. if that does not happen: if a result opens a company site, note that you have left indeed and the accessibility behavior may change. practice: open three results in separate tabs and compare them. 8.2 apply through indeed what you will learn: complete indeed-hosted forms and recognize employer-controlled steps. before you begin: open a suitable job. exactly how to do it activate apply now when available. confirm whether the application remains on indeed or redirects elsewhere. review contact/profile information. upload or select the intended resume. answer employer screening questions. review before submission. submit and save confirmation information. what should happen: the application is recorded and your tracker is updated. if that does not happen: if a screening step is inaccessible, use the accommodation/contact option where provided rather than guessing answers or asking someone to answer for you. practice: walk through a noncritical application up to the review step. indeed accommodation note: indeedâ€™s current disability-inclusion faq states that job seekers who require alternatives in searching, applying, interviewing, or hiring can seek assistance; the employer remains responsible for its own application and screening content. part 9 - company career sites and ats systems company career sites may use systems such as workday, taleo, icims, greenhouse, lever, successfactors, or custom portals. the exact labels vary, so use a structure-first workflow rather than memorizing one site. 9.1 orient to an unfamiliar application system what you will learn: find the important regions before typing data. before you begin: open the application in a desktop browser. exactly how to do it press h repeatedly to review headings. use landmarks/regions to find main, search, or application content. use f or your screen reader form-control list to identify text boxes, combo boxes, checkboxes, and buttons. find save, next, back, review, and submit controls before filling the entire page. identify whether the site autosaves or provides save and continue later. only then begin entering data. what should happen: you understand the page structure and recovery options before investing time. if that does not happen: if there is no reliable structure, use tab while taking notes on field order and save frequently. practice: map one unfamiliar application page without submitting. part 10 - online application forms 10.1 complete forms systematically what you will learn: prevent skipped fields and accidental submissions. before you begin: have your reusable information file available. exactly how to do it start at the first field. read the label before typing. enter only the information requested. use tab to move forward and shift+tab to recheck the previous field. for checkboxes, listen for checked/not checked before pressing space. for radio buttons, use arrow keys within the group. before next/submit, use your screen reader form-field list or shift+tab review to confirm required fields. use save/continue later when available. what should happen: required information is entered into the intended controls. if that does not happen: if a label is missing, use surrounding text, screen-reader object information, or request an accessible alternative rather than guessing sensitive information. practice: complete a practice form with text boxes, checkboxes, and radio buttons. part 11 - dropdowns, date pickers, autocomplete, and custom controls task how native combo box enter/alt+down to open when needed; arrow keys; enter to choose. autocomplete edit field type part of the value, then use arrow keys through announced suggestions and enter to select. date field prefer typing the documented date format when allowed; otherwise use keyboard navigation in the date picker. custom listbox listen for expanded/collapsed and selected state; arrow keys usually move within the list. slider arrow keys usually adjust the value; listen for the numeric state. toggle/switch space or enter; verify on/off state afterward. recovery habit: after choosing a custom control, shift+tab back once and listen to the selected value. dynamic applications sometimes accept focus movement without actually saving the selection. part 12 - resume parsing and re-entering work history ats resume parsing is not proof that every field was interpreted correctly. check employer names, job titles, dates, degree names, phone/email, and location carefully. re-enter information manually when required even if it duplicates the resume. do not write â€œsee resumeâ€ unless the application explicitly permits it. keep dates in one consistent format to reduce parsing errors. 12.1 audit parsed resume fields what you will learn: correct ats errors before submission. before you begin: resume upload has completed. exactly how to do it move to the first parsed field. compare it with your master resume. correct any split employer/job-title lines. check month/year dates. check that bullet accomplishments were not placed into employer/title fields. review education and certifications. save before leaving the page. what should happen: the application data matches the resume. if that does not happen: if parsing is severely broken, upload a simpler one-column resume version and try again if the site allows replacement. practice: audit one parsed application profile. part 13 - cover letters and application questions answer the question actually asked; do not paste a generic paragraph everywhere. use plain language and concrete examples. for â€œwhy are you interested?â€ connect the role, organization, and your relevant experience. for â€œdescribe a challengeâ€ use a short situation-action-result structure. keep a library of reusable examples, but tailor each final answer. do not disclose private medical information simply because a question asks about challenges or strengths. 13.1 paste long answers safely what you will learn: avoid losing text in unstable web forms. before you begin: draft the answer in word or a plain text editor first. exactly how to do it write and proofread the answer outside the application. copy it. return to the correct application field. confirm the label. paste. use ctrl+a inside that field only if you need to verify length/content, then cancel selection as appropriate. save the application page. what should happen: you keep a backup copy and reduce the risk of losing work. if that does not happen: if the site has a character limit, shorten the answer in the external editor before pasting again. practice: draft and paste one 150-word answer. part 14 - assessments and timed tests read the instructions before starting the timer. check whether the test requires video, drag-and-drop, visual pattern recognition, a specific browser, or locked-down software. test keyboard and screen-reader behavior before the timed portion if a practice item is available. if the assessment is inaccessible or extra time/another format is needed because of disability, request accommodation before starting when possible. do not ask another person to take an assessment for you. current platform note: indeed announced the discontinuation of its own assessments product, but employers may still send third-party pre-employment tests or screening systems. part 15 - requesting an application accommodation general u.s. principle: u.s. department of labor guidance states that qualified applicants may need reasonable accommodations to participate in the application process. examples can include alternate formats or adjustments to inaccessible recruiting/application technology. 15.1 request an accessible application method what you will learn: ask for a practical alternative when a barrier prevents equal participation. before you begin: document the barrier before contacting the employer. exactly how to do it write down the employer, job title, job id, application url, date, and exact inaccessible step. find the accommodation, hr, recruiting, or applicant-support contact listed in the posting/application. explain that you are an applicant and identify the job. describe the barrier functionally, such as â€œthe required assessment cannot be operated with my screen reader.â€ state the accommodation or alternative you need, such as an accessible version, extra time when appropriate, a keyboard-operable format, or another way to submit the same information. ask how the employer wants you to proceed. keep a copy of the request and response. what should happen: the employer has enough information to address access to the hiring process. if that does not happen: if the posting has no contact, use the company careers/hr contact or accessibility channel. for legal questions about rights, consult eeoc/jan or qualified counsel rather than relying on a recruiter for legal interpretation. practice: write a practice accommodation request for an inaccessible timed assessment. part 16 - disability disclosure and interview boundaries you do not need to put disability information on a resume unless you choose to and it is relevant to your goals. an accommodation request may require enough information to explain the need, but it does not require sharing unrelated medical history. in the u.s., pre-offer disability-related questions are restricted; employers may generally ask whether you can perform job functions and may discuss accommodation in appropriate circumstances. keep the conversation focused on job functions, access needs, and effective accommodations. eeoc guidance: eeoc states that an employer generally may not ask a job applicant disability-related questions before a job offer, though it may ask whether the applicant can perform the job and how the applicant would perform it, with or without reasonable accommodation. part 17 - job-search scams never pay to receive a legitimate job offer. be suspicious of interviews conducted only by text/chat with immediate offers and no normal hiring process. never deposit a check and send part of the money back for â€œequipment.â€ never buy gift cards or cryptocurrency for an employer/recruiter. check the recruiterâ€™s email domain and the employerâ€™s real careers site. compare the job posting with the companyâ€™s official careers page. be cautious when a recruiter moves the conversation to telegram, whatsapp, signal, or another private channel immediately. never provide banking information or identity documents before you understand why they are needed and have verified the employer. 17.1 verify a recruiter what you will learn: confirm identity through an independent path. before you begin: a recruiter contacts you unexpectedly. exactly how to do it read the full email address/domain. find the employerâ€™s official website by a known or independently typed address. locate the job on the official careers site if possible. check whether the recruiter appears on the company site or linkedin profile, but do not rely on profile existence alone. call or email the company through its official contact if the request involves sensitive information or money. what should happen: you know whether the recruiting contact is plausible before sharing sensitive data. if that does not happen: if the employer cannot verify the recruiter, stop the process. practice: verify a legitimate recruiter or staffing agency using public contact information. part 18 - email and recruiter communication use clear subject lines: â€œapplication - data analyst - job 12345 - your name.â€ keep replies concise and answer every scheduling/action question. read the full recipient address before sending sensitive documents. do not send social security cards, driverâ€™s licenses, bank details, or tax documents during ordinary early recruiting unless you have verified a legitimate onboarding process after an offer. keep copies of important recruiter emails in an application folder. part 19 - interview scheduling 19.1 confirm an interview what you will learn: record all logistics accessibly. before you begin: you receive an interview invitation. exactly how to do it read the date, time, time zone, platform, interviewer names, and meeting link. add the event to your calendar. add the job description or posting link to the calendar notes. if you need an interview accommodation, request it before the interview with enough lead time when possible. reply confirming attendance. one day before, reopen the meeting link only far enough to test the platform/deviceâ€”not to join unexpectedly if that would be inappropriate. what should happen: you have one reliable calendar record with all interview details. if that does not happen: if the invitation lacks time zone or platform, ask before the interview day. practice: create a practice calendar event from a sample invitation. part 20 - zoom, teams, and video interviews task how zoom test at zoom.us/test; know mute, camera, participants/chat, and leave controls. microsoft teams use the pre-join screen to verify microphone/camera; know mute, camera, chat, participants, and leave. google meet verify microphone/camera and know captions, chat, people, and leave controls. 20.1 prepare a video interview setup what you will learn: prevent platform navigation from becoming the interview itself. before you begin: know the platform. exactly how to do it update the app/browser before interview day. connect headphones/headset if you use them. test microphone and speakers. if camera is expected and you choose/use video, test camera framing with a trusted person or built-in preview. practice mute/unmute without searching menus. practice opening chat and participants, then return focus to the main meeting. know the leave command/control. close unrelated apps and silence nonessential notifications. what should happen: you can manage meeting controls without losing conversational focus. if that does not happen: if the platform is inaccessible, request an alternative or accommodation before the interview rather than improvising under time pressure. practice: run a ten-minute mock interview call. part 21 - interview preparation with a screen reader keep the job description in a separate document with headings for responsibilities, required, preferred, questions, and your examples. prepare five to eight short stories demonstrating skills using situation-action-result. use concise braille or text notes rather than a long script you must search during the interview. keep questions for the employer in a short numbered list. if using speech, use headphones so interviewers do not hear screen-reader output. if using braille, position the display so routing/typing noises do not interfere with the microphone. 21.1 build interview notes what you will learn: create notes you can retrieve quickly while listening. before you begin: open word or a plain-text editor. exactly how to do it create headings: role, company, three priorities, five examples, questions, closing. under each heading, use short bullet phrases rather than paragraphs. practice moving by heading with your screen reader. try answering one mock question while locating a note without long silence. what should happen: you can find a prompt quickly without reading a script word-for-word. if that does not happen: if note navigation is slow, reduce the notes until each section fits in a few lines. practice: run five mock questions using the notes. part 22 - after the interview immediately write down interviewer names, questions, commitments, and follow-up dates. send a concise thank-you email when appropriate. if you promised a portfolio/sample, send exactly what was requested through a verified address/link. do not assume silence means rejection; follow the stated timeline and then follow up once professionally. part 23 - application tracking and follow-up 23.1 update status after every contact what you will learn: keep the search organized across many employers. before you begin: open your tracker. exactly how to do it find the employer/job row. update status: saved, applied, recruiter screen, interview, assessment, offer, rejected, withdrawn, or other meaningful state. enter the date of the latest contact. enter the next follow-up date. add a short note with the person/contact and next action. what should happen: you can prioritize follow-ups instead of relying on memory. if that does not happen: if the tracker becomes large, sort/filter by next follow-up date or active status. practice: update five sample applications. part 24 - mobile job search linkedin and indeed mobile apps can be useful for searching and notifications, but long application forms are often easier on desktop with a physical keyboard. voiceover: use swipe navigation, rotor headings/forms, and double-tap to activate. talkback: use swipe navigation, reading controls, and double-tap to activate. keep the resume in files/drive/onedrive so it is available to mobile upload controls. for a complex inaccessible mobile form, switch to desktop before deciding the application cannot be completed. part 25 - troubleshooting inaccessible applications 25.1 you are tabbing forever what you will learn: switch from linear tab navigation to structure navigation. before you begin: a page has many controls. exactly how to do it press h to inspect headings. use landmarks/regions. use the screen reader forms list or f/form-control navigation. use browser find for â€œsubmit,â€ â€œnext,â€ â€œresume,â€ or the question text. return to tab only when you are near the intended control. what should happen: navigation becomes shorter and more predictable. if that does not happen: if the site exposes no useful structure, document the barrier and use the accommodation route. practice: navigate a long form without tabbing through every link. 25.2 focus jumps after you choose a dropdown what you will learn: reconfirm the selected value and your new focus location. before you begin: a dynamic control refreshed the page. exactly how to do it press shift+tab once. listen to the selected value/control label. press tab forward again. if focus returned to the top, use headings/forms navigation to return to the next required field. save if the application offers save. what should happen: you verify the choice before continuing. if that does not happen: if the selected value repeatedly disappears, capture the exact control label/problem and contact applicant support/accommodation. practice: practice on a country/state autocomplete field. 25.3 captcha blocks submission what you will learn: use the siteâ€™s accessible captcha or employer alternative. before you begin: a captcha appears. exactly how to do it look for an audio or accessibility alternative. use the providerâ€™s accessibility sign-in/cookie option if offered. refresh only if the alternative failedâ€”not repeatedly. if no accessible challenge exists, contact application support or request an alternative submission method. what should happen: you complete the human-verification step without asking another person to submit the application for you. if that does not happen: a sighted helper describing one inaccessible image may solve a one-time barrier, but a required inaccessible hiring process should still be reported/requested as an accommodation where appropriate. practice: identify the accessible alternative on a practice captcha page if available. 25.4 resume upload works but fields are blank/wrong what you will learn: treat upload and parsing as separate tasks. before you begin: the filename is attached. exactly how to do it confirm the uploaded filename. move through every parsed field. correct missing/wrong information manually. if replacement is allowed, try the simpler accessible resume version. save before proceeding. what should happen: the application contains accurate data even if parsing was imperfect. if that does not happen: do not submit based only on seeing/hearing the resume filename. practice: audit one parsed profile. 25.5 timed assessment is not accessible what you will learn: stop before consuming the timer when possible. before you begin: you discover a barrier before or at the beginning of the test. exactly how to do it do not continue guessing through inaccessible questions. document the exact barrier and test name. use the employer/test provider accommodation contact. request an accessible version or appropriate modification. keep the confirmation of your request. what should happen: the employer/provider can address access before the assessment is completed. if that does not happen: if the timer has already started, contact support immediately and document that the barrier occurred during the timed attempt. practice: write a sample barrier description. part 26 - independent practice course level 1 - workspace â˜ create job search folder. â˜ create tracker. â˜ create reusable information file. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 2 - resume â˜ check headings. â˜ run accessibility checker. â˜ create docx and accessible pdf copies. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 3 - posting â˜ find title/job id. â˜ extract required/preferred qualifications. â˜ save link and summary. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 4 - linkedin â˜ search. â˜ open result. â˜ review apply flow. â˜ inspect open to work visibility. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 5 - indeed â˜ search. â˜ open three results. â˜ distinguish indeed-hosted vs external application. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 6 - forms â˜ complete text, checkbox, radio, dropdown, autocomplete, and upload controls. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 7 - parsing â˜ upload resume. â˜ audit parsed work history. â˜ correct dates/titles. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 8 - writing â˜ draft cover letter paragraph. â˜ draft two application answers. â˜ paste/review safely. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 9 - accommodation â˜ identify an inaccessible barrier. â˜ write a functional accommodation request. â˜ find employer contact route. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 10 - interview tech â˜ test microphone/headphones. â˜ practice mute/unmute. â˜ open chat/participants and return. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 11 - interview notes â˜ create heading-based notes. â˜ answer five mock questions. â˜ ask three employer questions. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. level 12 - independence â˜ find job. â˜ evaluate. â˜ apply. â˜ track. â˜ schedule mock interview. â˜ follow up. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key, field, or next action to use. part 27 - quick reference checklists before applying â˜ read whole posting. â˜ confirm employer and job id. â˜ separate required vs preferred. â˜ save posting/link. â˜ choose tailored resume. â˜ check application deadline. â˜ check accommodation contact if you anticipate a barrier. before submit â˜ name/email/phone correct. â˜ resume filename correct. â˜ work dates correct. â˜ education/certifications correct. â˜ screening answers reviewed. â˜ attachments correct. â˜ no accidental disability/medical disclosure. â˜ confirmation/tracker plan ready. before interview â˜ date/time/time zone confirmed. â˜ platform tested. â˜ headphones/microphone ready. â˜ accommodation arranged if needed. â˜ job description and notes open. â˜ five examples prepared. â˜ questions prepared. â˜ notifications silenced. accessibility recovery pattern 1. stop. 2. identify the current page/field. 3. use headings/landmarks/forms navigation. 4. recheck state/selected value. 5. save. 6. try a desktop browser/known supported combination. 7. if the barrier remains, document it and use applicant support/accommodation. part 28 - official resources linkedin - find jobs with a screen reader linkedin - add open to options with screen reader support indeed - disability inclusion and accessibility indeed support - disability inclusion and accessibility faq u.s. department of labor - opening doors to all candidates eeoc - disability discrimination and employment decisions eeoc - tips for applicants with disabilities applying for federal jobs job accommodation network careeronestop final independence checklist â˜ i can organize a job search and track applications. â˜ i can produce an accessible resume in word/pdf. â˜ i can read a posting efficiently with a screen reader. â˜ i can distinguish required and preferred qualifications. â˜ i can search/apply on linkedin. â˜ i can search/apply on indeed. â˜ i can orient to unfamiliar ats/career sites. â˜ i can complete online forms and custom controls. â˜ i can upload and audit parsed resume data. â˜ i can draft and paste long application answers safely. â˜ i can identify when an assessment barrier requires accommodation. â˜ i can write a functional application-accommodation request. â˜ i understand basic disability-disclosure/interview boundaries. â˜ i can identify common job scams. â˜ i can schedule and prepare for video interviews. â˜ i can build accessible interview notes. â˜ i can follow up and track next actions. â˜ i can troubleshoot an inaccessible application without endlessly tabbing or guessing. most important habit: do not let an inaccessible application turn into a test of endurance. use structure navigation, save often, document the exact barrier, and use the employerâ€™s applicant-support or accommodation process when technology prevents equal participation. return to all manuals
